prize_parts.citation: for showing how collateral constraints and asset prices amplify and propagate economic shocks, providing the theory of credit cycles

statement.case_for: My configuration has changed. In round 1 I put B021 first and B002 as an alternative. I now put B002, confined to Kiyotaki and Moore, first. The change rests on three points from the exchange, not on support counts. First, I conceded in round 1 that the long-run verdict on the China-shock work is the main reason B021 is not an easy call. Boppart and Dreber, who both rate the evidence as strong, have moved away from it because of the tasks-and-trade bundle and the task-framework originators outside the credited names. The chair's summary shows I am the only explicit supporter. Taken together, these make me less confident that the achievement is both settled and cleanly bounded. Second, B002 meets the tests I care about. It has a single founding paper with two authors and no missing originator. It has nearly thirty years of use in theory, quantitative macro and policy modelling. Its core claim, that collateral values feed back on credit and turn temporary shocks into persistent ones, is about how societies absorb shocks, which is the question I value in B021. Third, the colleagues who argue for narrowing B002 (Boppart, Krusell, Teorell, and Hassler as a fallback) have removed the attribution objection. I do not use their agreement as evidence of merit. My ground is that the narrowed credit is the most bounded of the shortlisted achievements. On the chair's question about evidence, I would accept cross-episode historical evidence and firm-level evidence linking collateral values to investment and credit. I cannot verify the size of those effects from the supplied record, so I rest the case on originality, durability and breadth of use, and I do not claim the magnitude is settled.
statement.case_against: My own criterion is a long, public test against newly assembled data. B002 meets it less well than B021 does, because the theory's influence is greater than the direct identification of the size of the amplification. Colleagues from Boppart to Teorell note this. The 2022 prize on banks and financial crises is adjacent, and the Committee may judge the area honoured. I treat adjacency as a question of balance and timing and not as a scientific demerit. I would apply that principle to the 2008, 2022 and 2024 neighbours alike, and give it weight only where the discovery is not distinct. I also recognise that moving away from B021 leaves unrewarded the evidence that structural change imposes concentrated and persistent costs on places and workers. I still think that evidence deserves recognition once the long-run assessment is in.

responses.point: Hassler prefers Kiyotaki, Moore and Gertler, treating the accelerator and intermediary-based work as one connected insight about financial frictions. He keeps Kiyotaki and Moore alone as an acceptable fallback.
responses.response: In response to the chair's scope question, I would not support the three-name version, even with a citation written around financial frictions in propagation. His distinction between Gertler's later quantitative intermediary work and the 2022 recognition is reasonable. But it makes the achievement broader, and Gertler's credit is split with the eight-name B043. A bounded citation is easier to defend than one that depends on where his contribution is best placed. I welcome his statement that the two-name version is acceptable. The record does not show any evidence that separates the intermediary-based work from the 2022 recognition, so I am not persuaded that the third name is needed.

responses.point: Boppart keeps B002 to two names. He argues that the 2022 overlap is thematic, since banks and runs differ from collateral values in borrowers' balance sheets. He also moved B021 out of his preferred part because of the task-framework overlap and the unsettled persistence evidence.
responses.response: I agree with the distinction between the mechanisms and with the two-name scope, and I move toward his position. I take his reassessment of B021 as a fair challenge to what I wrote in round 1. Confining the citation to the China-shock core cleans up attribution, but it does not resolve the persistence debate. I still read that debate as one about magnitudes. I accept that it makes the case for waiting stronger than I admitted. I also share his candour that empirical identification of the size of amplification is weaker than the theory. I cannot say that B002 passes my testability criterion more strongly than B021 does. My claim is narrower: B002 has the cleaner boundary and longer maturity.

responses.point: Teorell proposes two parts: Kiyotaki and Moore for B002, and Pakes alone for B012. He uses the three-person cap as the reason to drop Gertler and credit one name in B012, and he accepts that Berry and Levinsohn are lost.
responses.response: I agree with his two-name B002 and with his reason for dropping Gertler. I do not support the pairing. Pakes alone drops Berry and Levinsohn from the demand-estimation breakthrough, and he records this as a real attribution loss. The two parts have no shared theme, as he also concedes. A second part adds attribution cost without obvious scientific gain, since B002 is already a bounded achievement. I would sooner look at B012 on its own terms as Pakes, Berry and Levinsohn. I also thank him for raising maturity earlier: he was right that the B021 verdict was still pending, and that is part of why I changed.

responses.point: Dreber ranks B025 first and B002 second. She says B002's empirical support for collateral amplification is thinner than the firm-level evidence behind B025, and she hesitates over B021 because it bundles two programmes.
responses.response: I take her empirical point seriously, because it is my own criterion. The firm-level tests of heterogeneous-firm models are extensive, and I keep B025 as an alternative for that reason. I still put B002 ahead for the cleaner two-author boundary. B025 omits Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum, which she accepts as a genuine attribution risk, and it sits next to the 2008 prize. On B021 I accept her bundling objection as the strongest reason for my change. I would only note that the objection could be met with a narrower citation if the Committee waits and the persistence evidence firms up.

uncertainties: How strong the evidence for quantitatively large collateral-driven amplification is. I cannot verify specific studies or magnitudes from the supplied record.
Whether the Committee reads the 2022 prize as covering the collateral-constraint mechanism or as complementary to it.
Whether, if B021 later matures, a China-shock core would survive the tasks-and-trade bundling objection and the Katz and Acemoglu-Restrepo attribution issues.
Whether B025 would be a better fallback than B021 once the omission of Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum and the Krugman 2008 overlap are weighed.
My comparison of the maturity of B021 and B002 depends on my own judgement of the post-2013 and post-1997 literatures. I have not independently verified citation or replication records.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile for the preferred B002 part (Kiyotaki, Moore) or for the alternatives B021 (Autor, Dorn, Hanson, Katz) and B025 (Helpman, Melitz, Redding). None of these people is among my listed co-authors. My work on electrification, railways and labour conflict is a field adjacency to B021, the ballot I ranked first at opening. I disclose it as a possible source of bias in my earlier preference. My profile lists collaboration with political scientists, including Johannes Lindvall, and notes that Jan Teorell was formerly at Lund. Both relate to B050, which is no longer in my configuration or alternatives. I also share Lund as an institution with Tommy Andersson, who supports B012. I disclose these without adjudicating them.
